blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS 1

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you began your exploration of the world of real numbers and encountered
irrational numbers. We continue our discussion on real numbers in this chapter. We
begin with very important properties of positive integers in Sections 1.2, namely the
Euclid's division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Euclid's division algorithm, as the name suggests, has to do with divisibility of
integers. Stated simply, it says any positive integer $a$ can be divided by another positive
integer $b$ in such a way that it leaves a remainder $r$ that is smaller than $b$. Many of you
probably recognise this as the usual long division process. Although this result is quite
easy to state and understand, it has many applications related to the divisibility properties
of integers. We touch upon a few of them, and use it mainly to compute the HCF of
two positive integers.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, on the other hand, has to do something
with multiplication of positive integers. You already know that every composite number
can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way — this important fact is the
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Again, while it is a result that is easy to state and
understand, it has some very deep and significant applications in the field of mathematics.
We use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic for two main applications. First, we
use it to prove the irrationality of many of the numbers you studied in Class IX, such as
$\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{5}$ . Second, we apply this theorem to explore when exactly the decimal
expansion of a rational number, say $\frac{p}{q}(q \neq 0)$, is terminating and when it is non-
terminating repeating. We do so by looking at the prime factorisation of the denominator
$q$ of $\frac{p}{q}$. You will see that the prime factorisation of $q$ will completely reveal the nature
of the decimal expansion of $\frac{p}{q}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So let us begin our exploration.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.2 The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a
product of its prime factors. For instance, $2 = 2$, $4 = 2 \times 2$, $253 = 11 \times 23$, and so on.
Now, let us try and look at natural numbers from the other direction. That is, can any
natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers? Let us see.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Take any collection of prime numbers, say 2, 3, 7, 11 and 23. If we multiply
some or all of these numbers, allowing them to repeat as many times as we wish,
we can produce a large collection of positive integers (In fact, infinitely many).
Let us list a few :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 5313$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 10626$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$2^2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 21252$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: and so on.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us suppose your collection of primes includes all the possible primes.
What is your guess about the size of this collection? Does it contain only a finite
number of integers, or infinitely many? Infact, there are infinitely many primes. So,
if we combine all these primes in all possible ways, we will get an infinite

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
collection of numbers, all
the primes and all possible
products of primes. The
question is – can we
produce all the composite
numbers this way? What
do you think? Do you
think that there may be a
composite number which
is not the product of
powers of primes?
Before we answer this,
let us factorise positive
integers, that is, do the
opposite of what we have
done so far.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We are going to use
the factor tree with which
you are all familiar. Let us
take some large number,
say, 32760, and factorise
it as shown.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So we have factorised $32760$ as $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$ as a product of
primes, i.e., $32760 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$ as a product of powers of primes. Let us try
another number, say, $123456789$. This can be written as $3^2 \times 3803 \times 3607$. Of course,
you have to check that $3803$ and $3607$ are primes! (Try it out for several other natural
numbers yourself.) This leads us to a conjecture that every composite number can be
written as the product of powers of primes. In fact, this statement is true, and is called
the **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic** because of its basic crucial importance
to the study of integers. Let us now formally state this theorem.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Theorem 1.1 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) :** *Every composite*
*number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation*
*is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.*

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
An equivalent version of Theorem 1.2 was probably
first recorded as Proposition 14 of Book IX in Euclid’s
Elements, before it came to be known as the
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. However, the
first correct proof was given by Carl Friedrich Gauss
in his *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae*.

Carl Friedrich Gauss is often referred to as the ‘Prince
of Mathematicians’ and is considered one of the three
greatest mathematicians of all time, along with
Archimedes and Newton. He has made fundamental
contributions to both mathematics and science.

Carl Friedrich Gauss
(1777 – 1855)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every composite number can
be factorised as a product of primes. Actually it says more. It says that given any
composite number it can be factorised as a product of prime numbers in a ‘unique’
way, except for the order in which the primes occur. That is, given any composite
number there is one and only one way to write it as a product of primes, as long as we
are not particular about the order in which the primes occur. So, for example, we
regard $2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7$ as the same as $3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 2$, or any other possible order in which
these primes are written. This fact is also stated in the following form:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The prime factorisation of a natural number is unique, except for the order
of its factors.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, given a composite number $x$, we factorise it as $x = p_1 p_2 ... p_n$, where
$p_1, p_2, ..., p_n$ are primes and written in ascending order, i.e., $p_1 \le p_2$
$\le ... \le p_n$. If we combine the same primes, we will get powers of primes. For example,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$32760 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Once we have decided that the order will be ascending, then the way the number
is factorised, is unique.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic has many applications, both within
mathematics and in other fields. Let us look at some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Consider the numbers $4^n$, where $n$ is a natural number. Check whether
there is any value of $n$ for which $4^n$ ends with the digit zero.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : If the number $4^n$, for any $n$, were to end with the digit zero, then it would be
divisible by 5. That is, the prime factorisation of $4^n$ would contain the prime 5. This is
not possible because $4^n = (2)^{2n}$; so the only prime in the factorisation of $4^n$ is 2. So, the
uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that there are no
other primes in the factorisation of $4^n$. So, there is no natural number $n$ for which $4^n$
ends with the digit zero.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already learnt how to find the HCF and LCM of two positive integers
using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic in earlier classes, without realising it!
This method is also called the prime factorisation method. Let us recall this method
through an example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 2 : Find the LCM and HCF of 6 and 20 by the prime factorisation method.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : We have : $6 = 2^1 \times 3^1$ and $20 = 2 \times 2 \times 5 = 2^2 \times 5^1$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You can find HCF(6, 20) = 2 and LCM(6, 20) = $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$, as done in your
earlier classes.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that HCF$(6, 20) = 2^1 =$ **Product of the smallest power of each common**
**prime factor in the numbers.**

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$$ \text{LCM } (6, 20) = 2^2 \times 3^1 \times 5^1 = \text{Product of the greatest power of each prime factor,} $$
$$ \text{involved in the numbers.} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From the example above, you might have noticed that HCF$(6, 20) \times \text{LCM}(6, 20)$
$= 6 \times 20$. In fact, we can verify that **for any two positive integers $a$ and $b$,**
**$\mathbf{HCF(a, b) \times LCM(a, b) = a \times b}$.** We can use this result to find the LCM of two
positive integers, if we have already found the HCF of the two positive integers.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:

find their LCM.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.3 Revisiting Irrational Numbers

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you were introduced to irrational numbers and many of their properties.
You studied about their existence and how the rationals and the irrationals together
made up the real numbers. You even studied how to locate irrationals on the number
line. However, we did not prove that they were irrationals. In this section, we will
prove that $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{5}$ and, in general, $\sqrt{p}$ is irrational, where $p$ is a prime. One of
the theorems, we use in our proof, is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall, a number ‘$s$’ is called \textit{irrational} if it cannot be written in the form $\frac{p}{q}$,
where $p$ and $q$ are integers and $q \neq 0$. Some examples of irrational numbers, with
which you are already familiar, are :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Before we prove that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, we need the following theorem, whose
proof is based on the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Theorem 1.2 : Let $p$ be a prime number. If $p$ divides $a^2$, then $p$ divides $a$, where
$a$ is a positive integer.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: *Proof : Let the prime factorisation of $a$ be as follows :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $a = p_1 p_2 \dots p_n$, where $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$ are primes, not necessarily distinct.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $a^2 = (p_1 p_2 \dots p_n)(p_1 p_2 \dots p_n) = p_1^2 p_2^2 \dots p_n^2.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, we are given that $p$ divides $a^2$. Therefore, from the Fundamental Theorem of
Arithmetic, it follows that $p$ is one of the prime factors of $a^2$. However, using the
uniqueness part of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, we realise that the only
prime factors of $a^2$ are $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$. So $p$ is one of $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, since $a = p_1 p_2 \dots p_n$, $p$ divides $a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We are now ready to give a proof that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The proof is based on a technique called ‘proof by contradiction’. (This technique is
discussed in some detail in Appendix 1).

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Theorem 1.3 : $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Proof : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text: * Not from the examination point of view.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we can find integers $r$ and $s$ $(\neq 0)$ such that $\sqrt{2} = \frac{r}{s}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Suppose $r$ and $s$ have a common factor other than 1. Then, we divide by the common

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: factor to get $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, $b \sqrt{2} = a.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get $2b^2 = a^2$. Therefore, 2 divides $a^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, by Theorem 1.2, it follows that 2 divides $a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we can write $a = 2c$ for some integer $c$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting for $a$, we get $2b^2 = 4c^2$, that is, $b^2 = 2c^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This means that 2 divides $b^2$, and so 2 divides $b$ (again using Theorem 1.2 with $p = 2$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $a$ and $b$ have at least 2 as a common factor.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But this contradicts the fact that $a$ and $b$ have no common factors other than 1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we conclude that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 5 : Prove that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $\sqrt{3}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: That is, we can find integers $a$ and $b$ $(\neq 0)$ such that $\sqrt{3} = \frac{a}{b}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Suppose $a$ and $b$ have a common factor other than $1$, then we can divide by the
common factor, and assume that $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, $b\sqrt{3} = a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Squaring on both sides, and rearranging, we get $3b^2 = a^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, $a^2$ is divisible by 3, and by Theorem 1.2, it follows that $a$ is also divisible
by 3.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we can write $a = 3c$ for some integer $c$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting for $a$, we get $3b^2 = 9c^2$, that is, $b^2 = 3c^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This means that $b^2$ is divisible by 3, and so $b$ is also divisible by 3 (using Theorem 1.2
with $p = 3$).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, $a$ and $b$ have at least 3 as a common factor.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But this contradicts the fact that $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that $\sqrt{3}$ is rational.
So, we conclude that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In Class IX, we mentioned that :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ the sum or difference of a rational and an irrational number is irrational and

$\bullet$ the product and quotient of a non-zero rational and irrational number is
irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We prove some particular cases here.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : Show that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

Solution : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is rational.

That is, we can find coprime $a$ and $b$ ($b \neq 0$) such that $5 - \sqrt{3} = \frac{a}{b}$.

Therefore, $5 - \frac{a}{b} = \sqrt{3}$.

Rearranging this equation, we get $\sqrt{3} = 5 - \frac{a}{b} = \frac{5b - a}{b}$.

Since $a$ and $b$ are integers, we get $5 - \frac{a}{b}$ is rational, and so $\sqrt{3}$ is rational.

But this contradicts the fact that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is
rational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we conclude that $5 - \sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 : Show that $3\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

Solution : Let us assume, to the contrary, that $3\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

That is, we can find coprime $a$ and $b$ ($b \neq 0$) such that $3\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$.

Rearranging, we get $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{3b}$.

Since $3$, $a$ and $b$ are integers, $\frac{a}{3b}$ is rational, and so $\sqrt{2}$ is rational.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: REAL NUMBERS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But this contradicts the fact that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we conclude that $3\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 1.4 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic :
   Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this
factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.

2. If $p$ is a prime and $p$ divides $a^2$, then $p$ divides $a$, where $a$ is a positive integer.

3. To prove that $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$ are irrationals.

blocks.text:
A NOTE TO THE READER

You have seen that :

$$HCF (p, q, r) \times LCM (p, q, r) \neq p \times q \times r, \text{ where } p, q, r \text{ are positive integers}$$
(see Example 8). However, the following results hold good for three numbers
$p, q$ and $r$ :

$$LCM (p, q, r) = \frac{p \cdot q \cdot r \cdot HCF(p, q, r)}{HCF(p, q) \cdot HCF(q, r) \cdot HCF(p, r)}$$

$$HCF (p, q, r) = \frac{p \cdot q \cdot r \cdot LCM(p, q, r)}{LCM(p, q) \cdot LCM(q, r) \cdot LCM(p, r)}$$
